title: Windrow House Rising Anew
premise: Estate lawyer Coral Hartwell is summoned to Windrow House to read a will for Edmund Vane, the town's beloved founder—except Vane died forty years ago, and when his grave is opened for the probate hearing, the coffin is empty. As Coral untangles the forged death certificate, a second body surfaces in the house's walled garden, and the killer begins feeding Coral anonymous pages from a case file that was supposedly destroyed in a fire. Coral, a trans man estranged from his own family, finds an unexpected found family in the Vane household's surviving staff and falls for the estate's archivist, Juniper, even as duty demands he treat them all as suspects. The trail leads to Vane's granddaughter, who faked her grandfather's death decades ago to escape an arranged marriage, and whose son has been killing to keep the secret buried; Coral traps him by leaking a falsified version of the case file, forcing a confession before the trial opens, and chooses to stay at Windrow House with Juniper rather than return to his old life.
about_author: Rosalind Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent a decade reading other people's last words before starting to write her own. She lives in a drafty converted carriage house with two cats and an unhealthy fascination with empty coffins.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Coral Hartwell, POV. Coral arrives at fog-shrouded Windrow House to probate a will dated last spring—signed by Edmund Vane, dead since 1984. The family lawyer insists it's a clerical error; the document's ink says otherwise. Coral feels the familiar pull of a puzzle and the unfamiliar chill of being watched. Beat: curiosity curdling into unease as the house seems to recognize him.

chapters.title: Exhumation
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. To validate the will, the court orders Vane's exhumation before a crowd of townsfolk. The coffin, lowered with ceremony, is opened to reveal only weighted sandbags and a rotted shroud. The crowd's grief turns to fear; Coral notices Juniper, the estate archivist, watching him rather than the grave. Beat: public shock, and Coral's first flicker of attraction amid the horror.

chapters.title: Pages from a Burned File
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. An envelope of typewritten pages arrives—excerpts from the original 1984 death investigation, a file officially destroyed in the courthouse fire. The pages contain details no living person should know. Detective Okafor warns Coral he's being set up as either bait or scapegoat. Beat: paranoia takes root; Coral realizes the killer is writing to him personally.

chapters.title: The Household of Strangers
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper introduces Coral to the staff who never left: the housekeeper, the groundskeeper, the cook—people bound to Windrow by loyalty and old debts. Coral, who left his own family after transitioning, feels the ache of a belonging he never had. Beat: found family warmth shadowed by the knowledge that one of them is lying.

chapters.title: A Body in the Walled Garden
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The groundskeeper's nephew is found strangled beneath the rose hedge, clutching a page of the burned file—the page naming Vane's granddaughter, Maren, as beneficiary. Okafor suspects the staff; Coral suspects the timing. Juniper goes pale and evasive. Beat: the mystery turns lethal, and trust fractures inside the house.

chapters.title: Maren's Silence
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral tracks down Maren Vane, now a frail recluse in a coastal convent, who admits her grandfather never died in 1984—he vanished, and she let the world believe what was convenient. She refuses to say more. That night Coral's cottage is ransacked and the file pages stolen. Beat: dread and the vertigo of realizing the case is older and stranger than a murder.

chapters.title: What Juniper Knew
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper confesses to Coral: she was hired years ago by Vane himself, alive and hidden, to curate the estate's true history. She kept his secret out of love and duty, and she believes his grandson, Theodore, discovered the deception and silenced him for good. Coral must weigh his duty as an officer of the court against protecting her. Beat: love declared in the space between confession and betrayal.

chapters.title: The Trap in the Case File
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral fabricates a false version of the file—planting evidence that Theodore's fingerprints were recovered from the coffin—and lets it 'leak' through the household. Only the killer could know it's false. Within a day, the real file pages resurface, altered, and Theodore requests a meeting to bargain. Beat: the hunter becomes the hunter; Coral's lawyer's cunning turns weapon.

chapters.title: Windrow House Rising
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, climax. Theodore lures Coral into the house's sealed east wing, intending to make him the file's final entry. Juniper and Okafor arrive as Theodore confesses—he killed his grandfather to keep the inheritance and the family name intact, then staged the will to smoke out loose ends. Coral survives by keeping Theodore talking, recording everything. Beat: terror, then catharsis as the trap closes.

chapters.title: Anew
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, resolution. The trial opens with Coral's recording as its cornerstone; Theodore is convicted. Maren, freed by truth, dies peacefully weeks later, leaving Windrow House to its staff. Coral, offered a partnership back in the city, chooses instead to stay—hired as the estate's counsel, building a life with Juniper among people who chose him. Beat: quiet joy; identity, family, and love all resolved on his own terms.
